Red Bull Racing.summary: Red Bull’s RB‑engine cover now has a tweaked central exit shape and a bigger rear‑corner duct (with optional blanks), boosting cooling reliability for the weekend’s hot track. The rear‑suspension fairing around the lower wishbone has been subtly reshaped, giving the car a steadier rear grip as it tackles the high‑speed corners. In short, these tweaks keep the power unit and rear end running smoother, so the team can focus on extracting pace rather than fixing problems.

Haas F1 Team.summary: Haas has tweaked the underside of the car, reshaping the floor panels to get a cleaner airflow and a better balance of down‑force. The change reduces drag on the straights while giving the rear more grip through the corners, so the drivers should be able to carry a little extra speed into turns and brake later. In short, it’s a subtle aerodynamic fix aimed at extracting more lap‑time without a major redesign, which could make a noticeable difference in qualifying and the race.

Racing Bulls / RB.summary: The RB’s halo shroud has been reshaped and its connection to the chassis re‑profiled, smoothing the air that passes over the cockpit. This tweak cuts turbulence and gives the aero package a small but useful boost in down‑force and cooling. The result should translate into a tighter, more stable car on the straights and through the corners for this weekend’s race.

Williams Racing.summary: Williams has tweaked the back‑most part of the front wing – both the flap and the endplate – to clean up the air that hits the car’s front and give the driver a steadier feel through the corners. The small aerodynamic adjustment should boost front‑end grip and improve overall balance, which is crucial for extracting lap‑time on a track where every fraction of a second counts. In short, a cleaner front wing means the car will be more stable and quicker around this weekend’s circuit.

Sauber / Audi.summary: Sauber‑Audi’s aerodynamic package stays exactly as it was – there are no new tweaks to the floor, rear wing or beam wing this weekend. In plain terms, the car will run on the same baseline down‑force and balance the team used in the previous race, so engineers can focus on set‑up and strategy rather than figuring out fresh aero changes. That means drivers won’t have to adapt to any surprise handling shifts and the team’s performance will hinge on tyre management and race‑craft.
